My mother kept a cigarette lighter in the kitchen drawer for thirty years without knowing how to smoke. It was a good lighter, brushed silver, with a dent in one corner. On one side somebody had engraved the name GORDON. Nobody in our family was named Gordon.

When I was nine, I asked her who he was.

“A man who had a lighter,” she said.

This was the sort of answer my mother considered complete. I went to my father, who said Gordon had been her first husband and a professional ballroom dancer. My father was washing a roasting pan at the time. He had to stop and sit down when I asked what had killed Gordon.

“The tango,” he managed.

For years I believed some portion of this. Not the tango, obviously, but the existence of a first husband. I pictured a thin man in evening clothes coming downstairs in our house, stepping over the spot where the carpet tack had worked loose.

The truth came out when we were packing my mother’s kitchen for her move to a smaller place. By then my father had been dead six years. I found the lighter under a layer of rubber bands that had gone brittle and stuck to the wood.

“Poor Gordon,” I said.

My mother looked up from wrapping a casserole dish. “Oh, for heaven’s sake. He installed the boiler.”

She told me he had left his lighter on the basement windowsill. She’d called the company, but Gordon had already gone to another job. They said they would tell him. A week later she called again. After that it seemed foolish to keep calling, but wrong to throw it out.

“Besides,” she said, “it was handy on birthdays.”

I turned the little wheel with my thumb. A spark jumped, startling us both.

In the new apartment there was one kitchen drawer narrow enough for cutlery, so everything else had to justify itself. We spent a pleasant, quarrelsome afternoon deciding what a person needed. Two corkscrews, she maintained, on the grounds that one was bad. I suggested keeping only the good one. She said you couldn’t tell which was bad until you used it. A glass lemon squeezer survived because she liked the weight. The electric knife went because neither of us could remember a meal improved by its participation.

At the end there was a shoebox of disputed objects. I took it home.

Last November, during a power cut, I went looking for matches and found Gordon’s lighter instead. It sparked but wouldn’t light. My daughter, who is twelve and has never seen anybody do anything as interesting as repair a small mechanical object, watched me take out the insert. Inside was a wad of pale cotton, dry as lint.

“What does it run on?” she asked.

“Lighter fluid.”

“Do we have lighter fluid?”

“No.”

We sat in the dark for a while. Across the street, a neighbor’s windows glowed an enviable gold. My daughter tried the wheel and got a spark on her third attempt. For that fraction of a second I could see the tip of her nose and her front teeth. She had the intent, slightly cross expression my father used to wear when threading a needle.

“Who’s Gordon?” she asked.

I nearly told her about the ballroom dancer. The shape of the joke was still there, waiting for someone to step into it. Instead I told her about the boiler man, the windowsill, her grandmother’s two phone calls.

“He must have wanted it,” she said. “It has his name.”

“Probably.”

“Maybe he’s still looking.”

I considered the odds. Gordon had installed our boiler in 1982. If he’d been young then, he might now be about my mother’s age. Perhaps there was a Gordon somewhere with a narrow kitchen drawer and no use at all for a lighter. Perhaps he had given up smoking the very day he lost it, and all the good years since were thanks to a basement windowsill in our old house.

My daughter set it on the table.

“You should get some fluid,” she said.

The lights came back before bedtime. The refrigerator shuddered into life, the oven clock began insisting it was noon, and upstairs a radio resumed a sentence it had started forty minutes earlier. I put the lighter beside my keys so I would remember.

It’s there now. On Saturday, if I think of it, I’ll take it to the hardware store. There’s a man behind the counter who knows what to do with things. He once spent fifteen minutes finding me a screw worth eleven cents. I expect he’ll open the lighter, test the wheel, and tell me whether the wick needs trimming. He may ask who Gordon is.

I have an answer ready.
